title: 1 Kings 20:13–21
context: A prophet promises Ahab victory so that he will know that the LORD is God, naming the young men of the provincial princes as the means. While Ben Hadad drinks in his tents, Israel routs the Syrian army, though Ben Hadad escapes.

verses.text: Behold, a prophet came near to Ahab king of Israel, and said, “The LORD says, ‘Have you seen all this great multitude? Behold, I will deliver it into your hand today. Then you will know that I am the LORD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: A prophet tells Ahab, “The LORD says, ‘Have you seen all this great multitude? Behold, I will deliver it into your hand today. Then you will know that I am the LORD.’” Arminian readers see God’s gracious initiative toward an unfaithful king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God acting for his name’s sake. The purpose clause “you will know that I am the LORD” shows that the deliverance aims at revealing God, not rewarding Ahab.

verses.text: Ahab said, “By whom?” He said, “The LORD says, ‘By the young men of the princes of the provinces.’ ” Then he said, “Who shall begin the battle?” He answered, “You.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab asks, “By whom?” and is told, “By the young men of the princes of the provinces,” and that he himself will begin the battle. Arminian readers see God working through unlikely instruments and calling Ahab to act.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God choosing modest means to display his power. Readers in this tradition note that the plan underlines that the victory comes from the LORD rather than Israel’s strength.

verses.text: Then he mustered the young men of the princes of the provinces, and they were two hundred and thirty-two. After them, he mustered all the people, even all the children of Israel, being seven thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab musters two hundred thirty-two young men and seven thousand Israelites. Arminian readers see Ahab obeying the prophetic word and preparing as instructed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a small force assembled at God’s direction. Many in this tradition note the number seven thousand also appears in 19:18, though the text does not draw a connection here.

verses.text: They went out at noon. But Ben Hadad was drinking himself drunk in the pavilions, he and the kings, the thirty-two kings who helped him.
verses.arminianNotes: They go out at noon while Ben Hadad is “drinking himself drunk in the pavilions.” Arminian readers see the enemy’s self-indulgence leaving him unprepared for the attack.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s providence in the timing. The contrast between Israel’s obedience and Ben Hadad’s drunkenness highlights how pride weakens judgment.

verses.text: The young men of the princes of the provinces went out first; and Ben Hadad sent out, and they told him, saying, “Men are coming out from Samaria.”
verses.arminianNotes: The young men go out first, and Ben Hadad is told, “Men are coming out from Samaria.” Arminian readers see the plan unfolding exactly as the prophet had said.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the prophetic word being fulfilled step by step. The narrative moves quickly, keeping the focus on the accuracy of God’s word.

verses.text: He said, “If they have come out for peace, take them alive; or if they have come out for war, take them alive.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ben Hadad orders, “If they have come out for peace, take them alive; or if they have come out for war, take them alive.” Arminian readers see careless arrogance from a drunken king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see an order that underestimates Israel’s force. Readers in this tradition note the irony that Ben Hadad plans captures while his own defeat is near.

verses.text: So these went out of the city, the young men of the princes of the provinces, and the army which followed them.
verses.arminianNotes: The young men and the army following them go out of the city. Arminian readers see Israel acting in faith on the word given, moving forward as instructed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see obedience to God’s direction. The repetition of “the young men of the princes of the provinces” keeps attention on the means God promised to use.

verses.text: They each killed his man. The Syrians fled, and Israel pursued them. Ben Hadad the king of Syria escaped on a horse with horsemen.
verses.arminianNotes: Each kills his man, the Syrians flee, and Ben Hadad escapes on a horse. Arminian readers see God granting victory as promised while Ben Hadad survives to return later.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s word fulfilled in the rout. The escape of Ben Hadad sets up the next campaign and the later question of how Ahab will treat him.

verses.text: The king of Israel went out and struck the horses and chariots, and killed the Syrians with a great slaughter.
verses.arminianNotes: The king of Israel strikes the horses and chariots with a great slaughter. Arminian readers see Ahab sharing in the victory God gave, though the narrative does not record his thanks.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the victory complete. Readers in this tradition note that the chapter keeps attributing the outcome to the LORD’s word rather than to Ahab’s strategy.
